entries.label: contested usage
entries.meaning: Strictly, *literally* means *exactly as the words say, not as a metaphor*. In everyday speech it is also used to intensify a figurative statement (*I literally died laughing*), which is almost the opposite sense.
entries.usage: The intensifier use is centuries old and is listed in major dictionaries, but many people find it sloppy, so avoid it in writing and at work. It is very common in casual speech, especially among younger speakers, and can sound exaggerated. The strict sense is still useful and fully standard: *The town is literally on the border*.
examples: The restaurant is **literally** across the street from our hotel, so we can walk there.
The word breakfast **literally** means breaking the fast of the night.
I've told you **literally** a hundred times to close the fridge!

drill.sentence: When Grandpa said he'd eat his hat if his team won, my little brother took it {{literally}}.
drill.hint: word for word, as exact fact (not *seriously*)

mistake.wrong: Our sales literally exploded in the last quarter.
mistake.right: Our sales grew dramatically in the last quarter.
mistake.why: In professional writing, the intensifier *literally* sounds careless, and read strictly it describes a real explosion.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *Actually* means *in fact* or *really* and often corrects or contrasts with what was expected. *Currently* means *now, at the moment*, which is the meaning of German *aktuell*.
entries.usage: Germans often say *actually* or *actual* for *aktuell* (*the actual version*), which confuses listeners: *actual* means *real*, while *current* means *present*. Americans also use *actually* to soften a correction or a surprise (*Actually, I'm from Ohio*). For *now*, use *currently*, *at the moment* or *right now*.
examples: I'm **currently** living in Denver, but I'm moving to Seattle in the spring.
I thought the movie would be boring, but it was **actually** pretty good.
**Actually**, the meeting is at three, not two.

drill.sentence: The museum is {{currently}} closed for renovations and will reopen next summer.
drill.hint: actually or currently? (at the present time)

mistake.wrong: The actual price of a bus ticket is $2.50, but it's going up next month.
mistake.right: The current price of a bus ticket is $2.50, but it's going up next month.
mistake.why: *Actual* means real, not present; German *aktuell* is *current* or *currently*.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *Eventually* means *in the end, after a long time or many delays*. German *eventuell* means *possibly* or *maybe*, which English expresses with *possibly*, *maybe* or *might*.
entries.usage: *Eventually* is sure about the final result and unsure only about when it comes (*She eventually agreed*). *Possibly* is unsure whether something will happen at all. In speech, *maybe* or *might* is more natural than *possibly* (*I might come later*).
examples: After three hours in line at the DMV, we **eventually** got our new licenses.
It's **possibly** the best pizza I've ever had.
Prices will **eventually** have to go up; our costs keep rising.

drill.sentence: Our flight was delayed four times, but we {{eventually}} landed in Denver at 2 a.m.
drill.hint: eventually or possibly? (in the end, after delays)

mistake.wrong: I will eventually come to the party, but I'm not sure yet.
mistake.right: I might come to the party, but I'm not sure yet.
mistake.why: *Eventually* means in the end and suggests it will surely happen; German *eventuell* is *might*, *maybe* or *possibly*.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *Sympathetic* means showing understanding and kindness about someone's problems, or supporting a cause. German *sympathisch* (pleasant, easy to like) is *likable* (also spelled *likeable*), *nice* or *pleasant* in English.
entries.usage: *A sympathetic doctor* listens and cares; *a likable doctor* is someone people enjoy being around. *Sympathetic to* also means agreeing with an idea or a group (*sympathetic to their demands*). In fiction, *a sympathetic character* is one the audience cares about, which comes closest to the German sense.
examples: My boss was very **sympathetic** when I told her my father was in the hospital.
Your new roommate seems really **likable**; where did you find her?
Many parents are **sympathetic** to the striking teachers, even though the schools are closed.

drill.sentence: When I told my landlord I'd lost my job, he was surprisingly {{sympathetic}} and gave me an extra month to pay.
drill.hint: sympathetic or likable? (showing understanding of my problem)

mistake.wrong: Your sister is very sympathetic; I liked her right away.
mistake.right: Your sister is really nice; I liked her right away.
mistake.why: German *sympathisch* is *nice* or *likable*; English *sympathetic* means understanding about someone's problems.

entries.related: *likeable* — the same word, the spelling preferred in British English; *nice*, *pleasant*, *easy to get along with* — everyday words for *sympathisch*.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *Sensible* means reasonable and practical, showing good judgment (German *vernünftig*). *Sensitive* means easily hurt or upset, aware of others' feelings, or reacting strongly to something (German *sensibel*, *empfindlich*).
entries.usage: Germans often say *sensible* for *sensibel*, which changes the meaning completely: *a sensible person* has common sense. *Sensible* is common for choices and things (*sensible shoes*, *a sensible decision*). *Sensitive* also describes skin, teeth, topics and data (*sensitive information*).
examples: Wear **sensible** shoes; we'll be walking on cobblestones all day.
He's a **sensitive** kid who gets upset when other children are left out.
It would be **sensible** to get a second opinion before the surgery.

drill.sentence: My skin is so {{sensitive}} that I can only use unscented soap.
drill.hint: sensible or sensitive? (reacts strongly, easily irritated)

mistake.wrong: My daughter is very sensible and cries at every sad movie.
mistake.right: My daughter is very sensitive and cries at every sad movie.
mistake.why: *Sensible* means reasonable and practical; German *sensibel* is *sensitive*.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *By Friday* means *no later than Friday*: the action happens at some point before the deadline. *Until Friday* means an action or state continues up to Friday and then stops.
entries.usage: German *bis* covers both, so learners often write *Please send it until Friday*, which sounds wrong. Use *by* with one-time actions (*finish, send, pay, arrive*) and *until* with continuing situations (*wait, stay, work, be open*). *Not until* means *not before* (*The store doesn't open until ten*).
examples: Please submit your expense reports **by** the end of the month.
The pool is open **until** 9 p.m. on weekdays.
Can you let me know **by** Wednesday whether you're coming to the barbecue?

drill.sentence: You have to return the library books {{by}} Tuesday, or you'll pay a late fee.
drill.hint: by or until? (no later than that day)

mistake.wrong: Please send me the signed contract until Friday.
mistake.right: Please send me the signed contract by Friday.
mistake.why: Sending is a one-time action with a deadline, so English uses *by*; German *bis* covers both words.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *Politics* is the activity of gaining and using power: parties, elections, debate and maneuvering. A *policy* is a specific plan, rule or course of action of a government or any organization; German *Politik* covers both.
entries.usage: *Politics* is usually singular (*Politics is…*), and it also means power games in any group (*office politics*). *Policy* is countable (*a new policy*, *two policies*) and is used for companies, schools and insurance (*a return policy*, *an insurance policy*). For a government's line on an area, say *foreign policy* or *energy policy*, not *politics*.
examples: I try not to talk about **politics** at family dinners.
The store's return **policy** gives you 30 days to bring items back.
Office **politics**, not performance, decided who got the promotion.

drill.sentence: The city's new parking {{policy}} lets residents park for free on weekends.
drill.hint: politics or policy? (a specific rule)

mistake.wrong: The government's energy politics has changed a lot since 2022.
mistake.right: The government's energy policy has changed a lot since 2022.
mistake.why: A government's plan for an area is its *policy*; *politics* is the activity of power and parties (German *Politik* covers both).

entries.label: US vs. UK
entries.meaning: In American English, *quite* before an adjective usually means *very* (*quite good* = very good). In British English, unstressed *quite* often means *fairly* or *somewhat*, so *quite good* can be faint praise.
entries.usage: Americans use *quite* mostly in somewhat formal or emphatic speech; in casual talk they say *pretty* (*pretty good*). With absolute adjectives, *quite* means *completely* in both varieties (*quite right*, *not quite finished*). When British colleagues call your work *quite interesting*, they may be lukewarm.
examples: Dinner was **quite** good; I'd definitely go back there.
I'm not **quite** ready yet, so give me five more minutes.
It was **quite** a surprise to run into my old roommate at the airport.

drill.sentence: There were {{quite}} a few people at the party, at least fifty, I'd say.
drill.hint: the word that turns *a few* into *a fairly large number*

mistake.wrong: My British supervisor said my draft was quite good, so it's ready to submit.
mistake.right: My British supervisor said my draft was quite good, so it may still need some work.
mistake.why: In British English, unstressed *quite good* often means *fairly good*, not *very good*.

entries.label: contested usage
entries.meaning: Something is *ironic* when the result is the opposite of what was intended or expected, often in a way that seems to mock the situation. Something is *coincidental* when two things happen together by chance, with no such reversal.
entries.usage: Many natives use *ironic* loosely for any odd or unlucky coincidence, a habit made famous by Alanis Morissette's song *Ironic*; careful speakers and editors object. Test it: a reversal of expectation (*the fire station burned down*) is ironic, while a surprising match (*two guests wear the same dress*) is a coincidence.
examples: It's **ironic** that the time-management workshop started 40 minutes late.
Any resemblance to real people in this film is purely **coincidental**.
The marriage counselor is going through a messy divorce; **ironic**, isn't it?

drill.sentence: My sister and I bought the same jacket on the same day; it was completely {{coincidental}}, since we hadn't talked in weeks.
drill.hint: ironic or coincidental? (a chance match, with no reversal of expectations)

mistake.wrong: It's so ironic that my best friend and I have the same birthday!
mistake.right: It's such a coincidence that my best friend and I have the same birthday!
mistake.why: Sharing a birthday is chance, not a reversal of expectations, so careful speakers call it a *coincidence*.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: An *opportunity* is a favorable chance to do something you want (*a job opportunity*). A *possibility* is something that might happen or be true; German *Möglichkeit* covers both.
entries.usage: If you can take it or miss it, it's an *opportunity* (*take the opportunity to*, *a great opportunity*). For likelihood or options, use *possibility* (*There's a possibility of rain*, *explore other possibilities*). Germans often say *I had the possibility to…*, which sounds odd; say *I had the chance* or *the opportunity to…*.
examples: Studying abroad was an amazing **opportunity** to learn Spanish and meet new people.
There's a real **possibility** that the game will be canceled because of the storm.
Let's use this **opportunity** to thank everyone who volunteered at the food bank.

drill.sentence: Doctors haven't ruled out the {{possibility}} of surgery, but they want to try physical therapy first.
drill.hint: possibility or opportunity? (something that might happen)

mistake.wrong: At my last job, I had the possibility to work with clients in Japan.
mistake.right: At my last job, I had the opportunity to work with clients in Japan.
mistake.why: A favorable chance you can take is an *opportunity* or a *chance*; German *Möglichkeit* often means *opportunity* in this sense.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: A *critic* is a person who judges or reviews something; *criticism* is the act or words of finding fault; a *critique* is a detailed, balanced evaluation. German *Kritik* corresponds to *criticism* or *critique*, never to *critic*.
entries.usage: Germans often say *I have a critic* for *ich habe Kritik*; say *I have some criticism* or *I have a few concerns*. *Criticism* is mostly uncountable and negative (*take criticism well*), while a *critique* is countable and more academic or artistic (*a critique of the plan*). *Critique* is also a verb: *Can you critique my essay?*
examples: The film was loved by **critics** but did poorly at the box office.
She takes **criticism** well, which makes her easy to coach.
Our writing group meets every week to **critique** each other's short stories.

drill.sentence: My only {{criticism}} of the hotel is that the walls were a bit thin.
drill.hint: critic, criticism or critique? (the everyday word for a negative comment)

mistake.wrong: I have one critic about your presentation: it was too long.
mistake.right: I have one criticism of your presentation: it was too long.
mistake.why: A *critic* is a person; the comment itself is a *criticism* (German *Kritik*), followed by *of*.

entries.term: beg the question vs. raise the question
entries.spoken_term: beg the question or raise the question
entries.label: contested usage
entries.meaning: Strictly, *beg the question* names a logical fault: an argument assumes the very thing it is trying to prove. In everyday use it usually means *raise the question*, that is, make people want to ask something.
entries.usage: The everyday sense (*which begs the question: who pays?*) is now very common in journalism and speech, but philosophers and many editors still object. In careful writing, use *raises the question* for that meaning and keep *begs the question* for circular reasoning. If in doubt, *raises* is never wrong.
examples: Saying the witness is honest because she says she never lies simply **begs the question**.
The new stadium is half empty, which **raises the question** of why the city built it.
The ad says the cream is the best because no other cream is as good, which **begs the question**.

drill.sentence: The latest rent increase {{raises the question}} of whether longtime tenants can afford to stay.
drill.hint: beg or raise the question? (makes people ask; the form careful writers use)

mistake.wrong: The delay begs the question: when will the bridge actually open?
mistake.right: The delay raises the question: when will the bridge actually open?
mistake.why: Careful writers keep *beg the question* for circular reasoning; to mean *prompts the question*, use *raise*.

entries.label: contested usage
entries.meaning: Today *decimate* means destroy or severely reduce a large part of something. Its original Latin sense was to kill one in every ten soldiers as a punishment.
entries.usage: The loose sense is standard in news and conversation (*decimated by disease*) and accepted by dictionaries; only a few purists still insist on *one in ten*. It works best for heavy losses in a group or population (*decimated the herd*, *decimated the team*). For complete destruction, *destroy* or *wipe out* is clearer.
examples: Ash trees across the Midwest have been **decimated** by an invasive beetle.
Injuries **decimated** the team's defense, so the coach had to start two rookies.
Streaming **decimated** the video rental business in less than a decade.

drill.sentence: Overfishing has {{decimated}} cod populations in the North Atlantic.
drill.hint: reduced drastically (the word from the Latin for *one in ten*)

mistake.wrong: The fire decimated the entire building, and nothing was left.
mistake.right: The fire destroyed the entire building, and nothing was left.
mistake.why: *Decimate* is best for heavy losses in a group or population; for the total destruction of one thing, *destroy* is the clear word.

entries.label: contested usage
entries.meaning: Both now mean *feeling sick, as if you might vomit*: *I feel nauseous*. Strictly, *nauseous* meant *causing nausea* (*a nauseous smell*) and *nauseated* meant *feeling nausea*.
entries.usage: *I feel nauseous* is what almost all Americans say, including doctors, and dictionaries accept it. Some editors and older speakers still prefer *nauseated* for the feeling, which sounds slightly clinical; for the cause, *nauseating* is now the normal word (*a nauseating smell*). In casual speech, *I feel sick to my stomach* and *I feel queasy* are also common.
examples: I always feel **nauseous** on boats, so I take something before a ferry ride.
The chemotherapy left her **nauseated** and too tired to eat.
A **nauseating** smell was coming from the dumpster behind the restaurant.

drill.sentence: The nurse's notes say the patient felt {{nauseated}} after taking the pills on an empty stomach.
drill.hint: nauseous or nauseated? (the form careful medical writers prefer for the feeling)

mistake.wrong: The smell at the fish market was really nauseated.
mistake.right: The smell at the fish market was really nauseating.
mistake.why: *Nauseated* describes a person who feels sick; a smell that causes nausea is *nauseating*.

entries.label: contested usage
entries.meaning: Strictly, *enormity* means great wickedness or the extreme seriousness of something bad (*the enormity of the crime*). It is often used loosely for huge size, where careful writers prefer *enormousness*, *immensity* or *magnitude*.
entries.usage: The loose sense (*the enormity of the task*) is very common and many dictionaries accept it, especially when the size is overwhelming. Still, many editors object, and *the enormity of her achievement* can sound like an insult. *Enormousness* is correct but clumsy, so most writers choose *size*, *scale* or *magnitude*.
examples: Only during the trial did the town grasp the **enormity** of what he had done.
As the floodwaters kept rising, the **enormity** of the disaster became clear.
No apology could make up for the **enormity** of the harm the company caused.

drill.sentence: It was months before the family understood the {{enormity}} of the fraud their accountant had committed.
drill.hint: enormity or enormousness? (the terrible seriousness of a wrongdoing)

mistake.wrong: We were amazed by the enormity of the new library; it has five floors.
mistake.right: We were amazed by the size of the new library; it has five floors.
mistake.why: Careful writers keep *enormity* for something terrible; for impressive size, use *size*, *scale* or *magnitude*.

entries.label: contested usage
entries.meaning: In its traditional dictionary sense, *peruse* means read something carefully and thoroughly. Many people use it to mean the opposite, browse or look through casually, which is closer to *skim*.
entries.usage: Because both senses are common and dictionaries list both, *peruse* is now ambiguous; many readers hear it as *browse* (*perusing the menu*). It also sounds formal or jokey in conversation. If precision matters, say *read carefully* or *study* for the first sense and *skim*, *browse* or *look through* for the second.
examples: I **skimmed** the article on the train but didn't have time to read it properly.
Please **peruse** the lease carefully before you sign it.
She spent the afternoon **perusing** the shelves of a used bookstore.

drill.sentence: I only had five minutes, so I {{skimmed}} the instructions and hoped for the best.
drill.hint: peruse or skim? (read quickly, only for the main points)

mistake.wrong: I perused the report in two minutes, so I missed the details.
mistake.right: I skimmed the report in two minutes, so I missed the details.
mistake.why: In its traditional sense, *peruse* means read carefully; a quick look for the main points is *skim*.

entries.label: contested usage
entries.meaning: Traditionally, *bemused* means puzzled or confused. Many people now use it to mean mildly or wryly amused, partly because it looks like *amused*.
entries.usage: Dictionaries now record the *wryly amused* sense, but many readers still take *bemused* as *confused*, so it can be ambiguous. Use *amused* or *entertained* when something is funny, and *puzzled* or *baffled* when you mean confused. A *bemused look* in fiction often mixes puzzlement with mild humor.
examples: The tourists looked **bemused** by the parking signs, which seemed to contradict each other.
The older kids were **amused** by the clown, but the toddler was terrified.
He gave a **bemused** shrug, clearly unsure what we were laughing about.

drill.sentence: The audience was clearly {{amused}}; people were laughing at every joke.
drill.hint: bemused or amused? (entertained, finding it funny)

mistake.wrong: I was bemused by your joke; it was hilarious!
mistake.right: I was amused by your joke; it was hilarious!
mistake.why: In its traditional sense, *bemused* means puzzled, so many readers would think you didn't get the joke.

entries.label: contested usage
entries.meaning: Traditionally, *nonplussed* means so surprised or confused that you don't know how to react. Many Americans use it to mean the opposite, calm and unbothered, which is *unfazed*.
entries.usage: The newer *unbothered* sense is common in American speech, and some dictionaries list it, but it makes the word ambiguous. To be clear, say *baffled* or *at a loss* for the original sense and *unfazed* or *unperturbed* for the calm sense. *Unfazed* is an everyday word, very common in sports and news (*unfazed by the pressure*).
examples: I was **nonplussed** when the clerk said my reservation didn't exist, even though I had the confirmation.
The goalie seemed totally **unfazed** by the noise from the crowd.
She stayed **unfazed** when the projector died halfway through her talk.

drill.sentence: His question was so strange that I was {{nonplussed}} and just stood there with my mouth open.
drill.hint: nonplussed or unfazed? (so confused you didn't know how to react)

mistake.wrong: The pilot was nonplussed by the storm and landed the plane smoothly.
mistake.right: The pilot was unfazed by the storm and landed the plane smoothly.
mistake.why: Traditionally, *nonplussed* means baffled; for calm and unbothered, say *unfazed*.

entries.label: contested usage
entries.meaning: *Disinterested* means impartial: having nothing to gain or lose, and so able to judge fairly. *Uninterested* means not interested, bored or indifferent.
entries.usage: Many natives use *disinterested* to mean *not interested*, and dictionaries record it, but careful writers and editors keep the distinction. The impartial sense is valuable in law, science and journalism (*a disinterested observer*, *a disinterested third party*). If you mean bored, *uninterested* or *not interested* is never criticized.
examples: We need a **disinterested** third party to settle the dispute over the fence.
The cat seemed completely **uninterested** in the expensive toy we bought her.
A judge should be **disinterested**, with no personal stake in the outcome of a case.

drill.sentence: My teenage son looked totally {{uninterested}} during the museum tour and kept checking his phone.
drill.hint: disinterested or uninterested? (bored, not paying attention)

mistake.wrong: The students seemed disinterested in the lecture and kept checking their phones.
mistake.right: The students seemed uninterested in the lecture and kept checking their phones.
mistake.why: In careful usage, *disinterested* means impartial; for bored or not interested, use *uninterested*.

entries.label: contested usage
entries.meaning: As a sentence adverb, *hopefully* means *I hope* or *it is hoped*: *Hopefully, the rain will stop*. Its older sense is *in a hopeful way*: *She looked at him hopefully*.
entries.usage: Usage writers attacked the sentence-adverb use for decades, but it is now standard, and the AP Stylebook accepted it in 2012. It is natural in speech, email and most writing; only a few very formal editors still avoid it. Like *frankly* and *honestly*, it usually comes at the start of the sentence or before the main verb.
examples: **Hopefully**, the rain will stop before the game starts.
The dog sat by the table, looking up **hopefully** at my sandwich.
We'll **hopefully** have the kitchen finished by Thanksgiving.

drill.sentence: {{Hopefully}} the package will arrive before we leave for vacation.
drill.hint: one adverb meaning *I hope that*

mistake.wrong: I'm hopefully that the flight won't be delayed.
mistake.right: I'm hopeful that the flight won't be delayed.
mistake.why: After *be*, use the adjective *hopeful*; the adverb *hopefully* comments on a whole sentence (*Hopefully, the flight won't be delayed*).

entries.term: I could care less vs. I couldn't care less
entries.spoken_term: I could care less or I couldn't care less
entries.label: contested usage
entries.meaning: Both mean *I don't care at all*. *I couldn't care less* is the logical original (my caring is already at zero); *I could care less* is a common American variant with the same meaning.
entries.usage: *I could care less* is widespread in casual American speech, but many people mock it as illogical, so it can make you sound careless. *I couldn't care less* is accepted everywhere and is the safe choice, especially in writing and with British listeners. Both are dismissive, so use them about things, not about people's problems.
examples: Honestly, I **couldn't care less** who wins the Super Bowl; I'm just here for the food.
My cat **couldn't care less** about the expensive bed we bought her; she sleeps in the box it came in.
"I **could care less** about awards," the actor told the reporter with a shrug.

drill.sentence: To be honest, I {{couldn't care less}} about fashion; I wear whatever's clean.
drill.hint: I could care less or I couldn't care less? (the safe, logical form)

mistake.wrong: In his newspaper column, the coach wrote that he could care less about the rankings.
mistake.right: In his newspaper column, the coach wrote that he couldn't care less about the rankings.
mistake.why: In edited writing and with British readers, the logical *couldn't care less* is the safe form; *could care less* is common in US speech but often criticized as illogical.

entries.label: usage trap
entries.meaning: *Regardless* means *without paying attention to* or *anyway*. *Irregardless* means the same, but its double negative (*ir-* and *-less*) makes it nonstandard.
entries.usage: *Irregardless* is in dictionaries and many Americans say it, sometimes as a joke, but it is widely seen as a mark of poor English. Don't use it in writing or at work; say *regardless*, *regardless of* or *anyway*. *Regardless* can also end a sentence (*We went regardless*).
examples: **Regardless** of the weather, the parade will go ahead on Saturday.
The tickets were expensive, but we went **regardless**.
Everyone gets the same bonus, **regardless** of how long they've worked here.

drill.sentence: {{Regardless}} of how tired you are, the dishes need to be done tonight.
drill.hint: irregardless or regardless? (the standard form)

mistake.wrong: Irregardless of the cost, we need a new roof.
mistake.right: Regardless of the cost, we need a new roof.
mistake.why: *Irregardless* is nonstandard because *ir-* and *-less* both make it negative; *regardless* is the correct form.

entries.label: contested usage
entries.meaning: As a verb, *impact* means *affect* or *have a strong effect on* (*The delays impacted sales*). It is very common in business and news, but some editors and readers dislike it.
entries.usage: The verb is now standard in American business writing, and *impacted* also has an old medical sense (*an impacted wisdom tooth*). Many style guides still prefer *affect*, which is simpler, or a precise verb such as *hurt*, *reduce* or *delay*. In formal writing, avoid piling up *negatively impacted* and *impactful*, which can sound like corporate jargon.
examples: The road closure will **impact** traffic on Main Street for about two weeks.
My dentist said my wisdom tooth is **impacted** and needs to come out.
Higher interest rates have **impacted** home sales across the country.

drill.sentence: Lack of sleep can seriously {{affect}} your mood and your memory.
drill.hint: impact or affect? (the plainer verb that careful editors prefer)

mistake.wrong: Smoking negatively impacts your health in many ways.
mistake.right: Smoking harms your health in many ways.
mistake.why: *Negatively impacts* is wordy jargon; a precise verb such as *harms*, *hurts* or *reduces* is clearer.

entries.label: contested usage
entries.meaning: *Is composed of* and *comprises* (without *of*) are the standard ways to say what something is made of. *Is comprised of* means the same and is very common, but many editors treat it as an error.
entries.usage: The traditional rule is that the whole *comprises* the parts, so *comprised of* is redundant. It appears in newspapers, laws and academic papers, and dictionaries record it, but copy editors still correct it. Safe choices are *consists of*, *is made up of* (casual) and *is composed of* (formal).
examples: The jury **was composed of** seven women and five men.
The national park **comprises** three islands and a strip of coastline.
The band **consists of** three brothers and their childhood friend.

drill.sentence: The new neighborhood is {{composed of}} about 300 homes, a school and a small park.
drill.hint: comprised of or composed of? (the form no editor would change)

mistake.wrong: The panel is comprised of three judges and two scientists.
mistake.right: The panel is composed of three judges and two scientists.
mistake.why: *Is comprised of* is common but widely criticized; use *is composed of*, *consists of* or *comprises* (no *of*).

entries.label: US vs. UK
entries.meaning: In American English, *momentarily* often means *in a moment, very soon* (*I'll be with you momentarily*). In British English, it means only *for a moment, briefly*.
entries.usage: The *very soon* sense is common in American service language, airports and offices, and the *briefly* sense is also used in the US (*I was momentarily confused*). British listeners may hear *We'll be landing momentarily* as a joke about landing for only a moment. If a sentence could be read either way, use *shortly* or *in a moment*.
examples: Ladies and gentlemen, we will be landing **momentarily**.
The lights flickered and went out **momentarily** during the storm.
Please have a seat; the doctor will be with you **momentarily**.

drill.sentence: Your table is almost ready, and the host will seat you {{momentarily}}.
drill.hint: the US adverb that means *shortly* here but *briefly* in Britain

mistake.wrong: Momentarily I'm working on a project in Munich.
mistake.right: At the moment I'm working on a project in Munich.
mistake.why: German *momentan* means *currently*; English *momentarily* means *for a moment* or, in the US, *in a moment*.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *Control* means have power over something or direct it (*control prices*, *control your temper*). *Check* means verify or inspect something, which is the usual sense of German *kontrollieren*.
entries.usage: Germans often say *control* for *check* (*Can you control my email?*), which sounds as if you want someone to manage or censor it. Use *check*, *verify* or *inspect*; *passport control* and *border control* are only fixed names for checkpoints. In research, *control for* a variable means hold it constant or adjust for it.
examples: Could you **check** my essay for typos before I send it?
It took him years to learn to **control** his temper on the court.
We **controlled** for age and income, so the effect isn't just about wealth.

drill.sentence: Before you leave, {{check}} that the stove is off and the windows are closed.
drill.hint: control or check? (make sure, verify)

mistake.wrong: The conductor controlled our tickets on the train.
mistake.right: The conductor checked our tickets on the train.
mistake.why: German *kontrollieren* is usually *check* or *inspect*; *control* means have power over or direct.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *Become* means *begin to be* (*become a doctor*, *become famous*). German *bekommen* means *get* or *receive*, so *I become a letter* says something absurd in English.
entries.usage: This classic false friend still slips out at advanced levels, especially in fast speech (*Can I become a coffee?*). For receiving, use *get* or *receive*; for ordering food, *I'll have* or *Can I get*. Before adjectives, *get* is the casual and *become* the more formal way to show change (*get tired*, *become clear*).
examples: She wants to **become** a nurse after she finishes high school.
Did you **get** my text about dinner tonight?
It's **getting** dark, so we should head back to the car.

drill.sentence: I {{got}} a lovely birthday card from my old piano teacher last week.
drill.hint: become or get? (received)

mistake.wrong: Excuse me, can I become a glass of water?
mistake.right: Excuse me, can I get a glass of water?
mistake.why: German *bekommen* is *get* or *receive*; *become* means turn into, so the sentence sounds as if you want to turn into water.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: English *also* means *in addition* or *too*. German *also* usually means *so*, *therefore* or *well* at the start of a sentence.
entries.usage: Starting a sentence with *Also,…* in English adds a new point (*Also, the hotel has a pool*); it never draws a conclusion. To conclude, say *so*, *therefore* (formal) or *that means*; to start talking, say *so* or *well*. *Also* usually goes before the main verb (*She also speaks French*), while *too* goes at the end.
examples: The apartment is close to the subway, and it **also** has a small balcony.
The store was closed, **so** we ordered the part online.
**So**, how was your trip to Mexico?

drill.sentence: The bridge is closed for repairs, {{so}} we'll have to take the long way around.
drill.hint: also or so? (therefore, introducing a result)

mistake.wrong: The train was canceled. Also, we took a taxi.
mistake.right: The train was canceled, so we took a taxi.
mistake.why: German *also* means *so* or *therefore*; English *also* only adds information.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *Meaning* is what a word, sign or event signifies. Your *opinion* is what you think about something, which is German *Meinung*.
entries.usage: *In my meaning* is a typical German error; say *in my opinion*, *I think*, or in speech *if you ask me*. Watch the verb too: *mean* is *signify* or *intend* (*What do you mean?*), while German *meinen* is often *think* (*Was meinst du?* can be *What do you think?*).
examples: What's the **meaning** of that orange light on the dashboard?
In my **opinion**, the book was better than the movie.
Everyone in the family has an **opinion** about where we should go on vacation.

drill.sentence: If you want my honest {{opinion}}, the blue dress looks better on you.
drill.hint: meaning or opinion? (what I think)

mistake.wrong: In my meaning, we should leave earlier to avoid the traffic.
mistake.right: In my opinion, we should leave earlier to avoid the traffic.
mistake.why: German *Meinung* is *opinion*; *meaning* is what something signifies.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *Consistent* means always behaving or happening in the same way, which covers the main sense of German *konsequent*. *Consequent* means *resulting from something* and is rare and formal (*the storm and the consequent flooding*).
entries.usage: Germans often say *consequent* for *konsequent*, but English listeners won't hear it as praise. For *konsequent* in parenting or rules, say *consistent* (*Be consistent about bedtime*); for following through firmly, say *firm* or *follow through*. *Consequently* is common and means *as a result*.
examples: Kids do better when parents are **consistent** about rules and bedtimes.
Her race times have been remarkably **consistent** all season.
Heavy rain caused a landslide and the **consequent** closure of the highway.

drill.sentence: If you tell the dog no on Monday and let him on the couch on Tuesday, you're not being {{consistent}}.
drill.hint: consistent or consequent? (acting the same way every time)

mistake.wrong: You have to be consequent with your kids, or they won't take the rules seriously.
mistake.right: You have to be consistent with your kids, or they won't take the rules seriously.
mistake.why: German *konsequent* is usually *consistent* or *firm*; English *consequent* only means resulting.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *Reputable* means trustworthy and respected, with a good reputation, which is often German *seriös*. *Serious* means grave or important, or not joking.
entries.usage: *A serious company* in English sounds like a company that doesn't joke, not one you can trust. For businesses, sources and professionals, use *reputable*, *trustworthy*, *legitimate* or *established* (*a reputable dealer*). *Serious* is right for problems, illnesses and intentions (*a serious injury*, *Are you serious?*).
examples: Always buy a used car from a **reputable** dealer, not from a stranger online.
Luckily, the injury wasn't **serious**, and he was back on the field a week later.
Check the story against a **reputable** news source before you share it.

drill.sentence: We only hire movers from a {{reputable}} company with good reviews and proper insurance.
drill.hint: serious or reputable? (trustworthy, with a good name)

mistake.wrong: This website looks serious; I think we can order from it.
mistake.right: This website looks reputable; I think we can order from it.
mistake.why: German *seriös* is *reputable* or *legitimate*; *serious* means grave or not joking.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: German *Engagement* (dedication, active involvement) is usually *commitment* or *dedication* in English. English *engagement* is a promise to marry, a formal appointment, or involvement and interest (*student engagement*).
entries.usage: *Thank you for your engagement* sounds odd to Americans; say *Thank you for your commitment* or *for all your hard work*. *Engagement* is natural in marketing and education (*engagement rate*, *student engagement*), but it is weaker than *commitment*. The verb *sich engagieren* is *get involved*, *volunteer* or *be committed to*.
examples: They announced their **engagement** at her parents' anniversary party.
Her **commitment** to the team is obvious; she comes to every practice, even when she's sick.
Teachers say student **engagement** drops sharply after lunch.

drill.sentence: Thank you for your {{commitment}} to this animal shelter over the past ten years.
drill.hint: engagement or commitment? (dedication over a long time)

mistake.wrong: Thanks to her engagement for the club, we raised $10,000.
mistake.right: Thanks to her commitment to the club, we raised $10,000.
mistake.why: German *Engagement für* is *commitment to* or *dedication to*; English *engagement* more often means a promise to marry.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *Irritated* means annoyed or impatient, or (of skin and eyes) red and sore. German *irritiert* often means *confused*, *puzzled* or *thrown off*, which English expresses with those words.
entries.usage: *I was irritated by his comment* means it annoyed you, not that it puzzled you, so this false friend can cause real misunderstandings. For the German sense, say *confused*, *puzzled*, *thrown* or *taken aback*. *Irritating* describes the thing that annoys you (*an irritating noise*).
examples: I was a little **confused** by the directions, so I called our host.
He gets **irritated** when people walk slowly in front of him on the sidewalk.
The new soap left my skin red and **irritated**.

drill.sentence: The map showed a road that didn't exist, and I was totally {{confused}} about which way to go.
drill.hint: irritated or confused? (unsure, puzzled)

mistake.wrong: Her email irritated me; I didn't understand what she wanted.
mistake.right: Her email confused me; I didn't understand what she wanted.
mistake.why: German *irritieren* often means *confuse* or *puzzle*; English *irritate* means annoy.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *Subtle* means delicate, understated or not obvious (German *dezent*). *Decent* means acceptable or good enough (*a decent salary*), or morally good and respectable (*a decent person*).
entries.usage: Germans often say *decent* for *dezent* (*decent makeup*, *decent colors*), which English listeners hear as *acceptable* or *not indecent*. For the German sense, use *subtle*, *understated*, *muted* or *discreet* (*subtle makeup*, *a muted gray*). *Decent* is a common, warm word for adequate quality (*The food was decent*).
examples: She wore **subtle** makeup and a simple black dress to the interview.
We found a **decent** hotel near the station for under $100 a night.
He's a **decent** guy; he returned the wallet with all the cash still in it.

drill.sentence: I like the new logo; the colors are {{subtle}} but still stand out on a white background.
drill.hint: decent or subtle? (understated, not loud)

mistake.wrong: I prefer decent colors for the living room, like light gray or beige.
mistake.right: I prefer subtle colors for the living room, like light gray or beige.
mistake.why: German *dezent* is *subtle* or *understated*; *decent* means acceptable or morally good.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *Oversee* means supervise or be in charge of work or people. *Overlook* means fail to notice something, which is German *übersehen*; it can also mean have a view over a place.
entries.usage: German *übersehen* looks like *oversee* but means *overlook* or *miss*, so *I oversaw the error* sounds as if you supervised it. *Overlook* has three uses: fail to notice (*overlook a detail*), deliberately ignore or forgive (*overlook it this once*), and look down on a place (*a room overlooking the lake*). *Oversee* is formal; in speech, *supervise* or *be in charge of* is more common.
examples: She **oversees** a team of 20 nurses on the night shift.
Our hotel room **overlooked** the harbor, so we watched the boats every morning.
It's easy to **overlook** a small leak until the water bill arrives.

drill.sentence: Sorry, I {{overlooked}} your message; it went straight to my spam folder.
drill.hint: oversee or overlook? (failed to notice)

mistake.wrong: Sorry, I oversaw your question in the email.
mistake.right: Sorry, I overlooked your question in the email.
mistake.why: German *übersehen* is *overlook* or *miss*; *oversee* means supervise.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: A *projector* is the device that shows slides or video on a wall or screen; Germans call it a *Beamer*. In American slang, a *Beamer* or *Beemer* is a BMW.
entries.usage: Say *projector* at work and at school; *beamer* will confuse Americans or make them think of a car. Other German pseudo-English words in the same trap include *Handy* (*cell phone*) and *Oldtimer* (*classic car*).
examples: Can someone help me connect my laptop to the **projector**?
The classroom **projector** keeps overheating, so the teacher uses the TV instead.
My neighbor just bought a used **Beamer**, and he washes it every Sunday.

drill.sentence: We watched the game on a big sheet in the backyard using an old {{projector}}.
drill.hint: beamer or projector? (the English word for the device)

mistake.wrong: The beamer in Room 4 isn't working.
mistake.right: The projector in Room 4 isn't working.
mistake.why: *Beamer* is German pseudo-English; in American English it's a *projector*, and *Beamer* is slang for a BMW.

entries.term: home office vs. working from home
entries.spoken_term: home office or working from home
entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *Working from home* (often *WFH* in writing) is the activity of doing your job at home, German *Homeoffice*. A *home office* is a room or area in your home set up for work.
entries.usage: Germans say *I'm in home office today*, which sounds wrong in English; say *I'm working from home today* or *I'm remote today*. Use *home office* only for the space (*We turned the guest room into a home office*). In the US, *home office* can also mean a company's headquarters (*the home office in Atlanta*).
examples: I'm **working from home** tomorrow, so call my cell instead of my desk phone.
We turned the spare bedroom into a **home office** with a standing desk.
Many parents found **working from home** with small kids nearly impossible.

drill.sentence: I can't come into the office today; I'm {{working from home}} because the plumber is coming.
drill.hint: home office or working from home? (the activity of doing your job at home)

mistake.wrong: I'm in home office on Mondays and Fridays.
mistake.right: I work from home on Mondays and Fridays.
mistake.why: German *Homeoffice* is *working from home*; an English *home office* is a room.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: A *physician* is a medical doctor (German *Arzt*). A *physicist* is a scientist who studies physics (German *Physiker*).
entries.usage: Because German *Physiker* looks like *physician*, this mix-up is common and can be embarrassing in introductions. In everyday American English, people say *doctor*; *physician* is more formal and common in medicine and insurance (*primary care physician*). The stress differs: phy-SI-cian, but PHYS-i-cist.
examples: My **physician** referred me to a specialist for my knee.
My brother is a **physicist**, so he can explain why the sky is blue.
The hospital is hiring two more **physicians** for its rural clinics.

drill.sentence: Einstein is probably the most famous {{physicist}} in history.
drill.hint: physician or physicist? (a physics scientist)

mistake.wrong: My father is a physician; he works at CERN on particle detectors.
mistake.right: My father is a physicist; he works at CERN on particle detectors.
mistake.why: German *Physiker* is *physicist*; a *physician* is a medical doctor (*Arzt*).

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: German *Promotion* (earning a doctoral degree) is a *doctorate* or *PhD* in English. An English *promotion* is a move to a higher job, or a marketing campaign or sale.
entries.usage: *After my promotion, I moved to Boston* makes Americans think you got a better job. Say *after my PhD* or *after I finished my doctorate*; the verb *promovieren* is *do a PhD* or *earn a doctorate*. A *Doktorand* is a *PhD student* or *doctoral candidate*.
examples: She got a **promotion** to senior manager after only two years.
He spent five years on his **doctorate** in chemistry before moving into industry.
The store is running a **promotion**: buy one pizza, get one free.

drill.sentence: After eight years at the bank, he finally got the {{promotion}} he'd been hoping for.
drill.hint: promotion or doctorate? (a move to a higher job)

mistake.wrong: I did my promotion at the University of Heidelberg.
mistake.right: I did my PhD at the University of Heidelberg.
mistake.why: German *Promotion* is a *PhD* or *doctorate*; an English *promotion* is a better job or a sales campaign.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: A *technique* is a method or skill for doing something (*a breathing technique*). *Technology* is machines, devices and the knowledge behind them; German *Technik* covers both, and also *engineering*.
entries.usage: Germans often say *technique* where English needs *technology* (*the technique in this car*). Ask: is it a way of doing something (*technique*), or tools and systems (*technology*)? As a field of study, *Technik* is usually *engineering*; the adjective *technisch* is *technical* or, for devices and systems, *technological*.
examples: My swim coach helped me fix my breathing **technique**.
Our hospital just bought new imaging **technology** that cuts scan times in half.
My grandparents struggle with **technology**, so I set up their new phone for them.

drill.sentence: The chef showed us a simple {{technique}} for chopping onions without crying.
drill.hint: technique or technology? (a method or skill)

mistake.wrong: The technique in this car is very modern.
mistake.right: The technology in this car is very modern.
mistake.why: Devices and systems are *technology*; *technique* is a person's method or skill (both German *Technik*).

entries.label: usage trap
entries.meaning: In everyday English, *significant* means large or important. *Statistically significant* means that a result is unlikely to be due to chance alone, even if the effect is tiny and unimportant.
entries.usage: In research writing, many editors want *significant* reserved for the statistical sense, so write *substantial*, *large* or *important* for size. In news and talks, *significant* alone usually means *big*, which leads to misreadings of studies. A careful phrase is *statistically significant but small*.
examples: The drug's effect was **statistically significant** but too small to matter for most patients.
Moving to a new city is a **significant** decision, so take your time.
There's been a **significant** increase in bike thefts downtown this year.

drill.sentence: Losing his job was a {{significant}} blow to the family's finances.
drill.hint: significant or statistically significant? (the everyday sense: large and important)

mistake.wrong: The study found a significant effect, so the pill clearly works well.
mistake.right: The study found a statistically significant effect, but it may be too small to matter.
mistake.why: *Statistically significant* means unlikely to be chance, not large or important.

entries.label: usage trap
entries.meaning: In everyday speech, a *theory* is a guess or hunch (*I have a theory about why he left*). In science, a *theory* is a broad, well-tested explanation supported by a lot of evidence, such as the theory of relativity.
entries.usage: The two senses are often confused in public debate: *it's just a theory* treats a scientific theory as a mere guess. In science, a testable guess is a *hypothesis*, and a *theory* is far stronger. In casual speech, *my theory is…* is perfectly natural and often humorous.
examples: My **theory** is that the cat knocks things off the table just to get attention.
Germ **theory** explains how bacteria and viruses cause disease.
Detectives had a **theory** about the break-in but no evidence to back it up.

drill.sentence: Grandma has a {{theory}} that it always rains the day after she washes her car.
drill.hint: everyday sense: an unproven personal explanation (in science, a well-tested one)

mistake.wrong: It's only a theory, so scientists are still testing whether it's true.
mistake.right: It's only a hypothesis, so scientists are still testing whether it's true.
mistake.why: In science, an idea that is still being tested is a *hypothesis*; a *theory* is a well-supported explanation, not a guess.

entries.label: usage trap
entries.meaning: In mathematics, something grows *exponentially* when it multiplies by a constant factor in each time period, such as doubling every year. In everyday speech, *exponentially* often just means *very fast* or *much more*.
entries.usage: The loose use (*It's exponentially better*) is common in speech, ads and business talk, but it annoys scientists and engineers, and it makes no sense for a single comparison (*exponentially bigger*), where nothing grows over time. In technical writing, use it only for real exponential growth; otherwise say *rapidly*, *dramatically* or *many times over*.
examples: Early in an epidemic, case numbers can grow **exponentially**, doubling every few days.
With compound interest, your savings grow **exponentially** over the decades.
Once the video went viral, the number of views rose **exponentially**.

drill.sentence: Bacteria in warm food can multiply {{exponentially}}, doubling every 20 minutes or so.
drill.hint: in the strict math sense: by a constant factor in each period

mistake.wrong: Our new office is exponentially bigger than the old one.
mistake.right: Our new office is much bigger than the old one.
mistake.why: *Exponentially* describes growth over time by a constant factor; for a single comparison, use *much*, *far* or *many times*.

entries.label: usage trap
entries.meaning: A *method* is a specific procedure or technique used to do something. *Methodology* is the study of methods, or the overall approach and the reasons behind the methods a study uses.
entries.usage: In academic and business writing, *methodology* is often used as a grander word for *method* (*our methodology was a survey*), and many editors object. Use *method* for what you did and *methodology* when you discuss and justify your approach. In journal articles, the section is usually called *Methods*.
examples: My grandmother's **method** for pie crust involves ice water and very cold butter.
The poll's **methodology** was criticized because it only reached people with landlines.
We used the same **method** to measure blood pressure at every visit.

drill.sentence: There's no single {{method}} for teaching a toddler to sleep through the night.
drill.hint: method or methodology? (one practical way of doing something)

mistake.wrong: Our methodology was to call 200 customers and ask them five questions.
mistake.right: Our method was to call 200 customers and ask them five questions.
mistake.why: A concrete procedure is a *method*; *methodology* is the reasoning behind methods, so using it for *method* sounds inflated.

entries.label: usage trap
entries.meaning: *Penultimate* means *second to last* (*the penultimate episode*). It is sometimes wrongly used as a fancier *ultimate*, meaning *the very best* or *the most extreme*.
entries.usage: *Penultimate* is formal; in conversation, *second to last* or *next to last* is more common. *Ultimate* means *final* or *the greatest example of its kind* (*the ultimate goal*, *the ultimate road trip*). Adding *pen-* does not make it stronger; it makes it one step before the end.
examples: She was eliminated in the **penultimate** round, just one step from the final.
The **penultimate** chapter is where the whole mystery finally makes sense.
On a cold winter night, mac and cheese is the **ultimate** comfort food.

drill.sentence: We missed the {{penultimate}} train of the night, so we had to wait an hour for the very last one.
drill.hint: penultimate or ultimate? (second to last)

mistake.wrong: This is the penultimate guide to Paris; everything you need is here.
mistake.right: This is the ultimate guide to Paris; everything you need is here.
mistake.why: *Penultimate* means second to last; the very best or most complete is *ultimate*.

entries.label: contested usage
entries.meaning: Strictly, *fortuitous* means happening by chance, whether the result is good or bad. It is now widely used to mean *lucky*, especially for a lucky accident.
entries.usage: Most uses today combine both ideas (*a fortuitous meeting* is a lucky accident), and dictionaries accept the *lucky* sense, though some editors still object. *Fortuitous* describes events, not people, and it needs an element of chance; for simple good luck, *fortunate* or *lucky* is clearer. In speech, *lucky* is the most common word.
examples: Our meeting was entirely **fortuitous**: we had both missed the same connecting flight.
We were **fortunate** to find a pediatrician who still accepts new patients.
The discovery of penicillin was partly **fortuitous**: Fleming had left a dish of bacteria out during his vacation.

drill.sentence: I feel very {{fortunate}} to have such supportive parents.
drill.hint: fortuitous or fortunate? (lucky; said about a person, with no chance event)

mistake.wrong: We were fortuitous to get tickets before they sold out.
mistake.right: We were fortunate to get tickets before they sold out.
mistake.why: *Fortuitous* describes an event, not a person; people are *fortunate* or *lucky*.

entries.label: usage trap
entries.meaning: The verb *sanction* has two almost opposite senses: officially approve or allow something (*a race sanctioned by the federation*), and impose a penalty (*the regulator sanctioned the bank*). The plural noun *sanctions* usually means penalties, especially against a country.
entries.usage: Context decides: *officially sanctioned* and *a sanctioned event* mean approved, while *sanctions against a country* and *the player was sanctioned* mean penalties. When the object is a person, company or country, the verb usually means *penalize*; when it is an action or event, it usually means *approve*. If there is any doubt, say *approve* or *penalize* instead.
examples: The race is officially **sanctioned**, so finishing times count for national rankings.
The state medical board **sanctioned** the doctor for prescribing painkillers without proper exams.
Several countries imposed economic **sanctions** after the military coup.

drill.sentence: The tournament isn't {{sanctioned}} by the tennis association, so the results won't affect anyone's ranking.
drill.hint: the formal verb that can mean either approve or penalize; here, the positive sense

mistake.wrong: The company was sanctioned to sell the drug in Europe.
mistake.right: The company was approved to sell the drug in Europe.
mistake.why: When a person or company is *sanctioned*, it usually means penalized; for permission, say *approved* or *authorized*.

entries.label: usage trap
entries.meaning: *Oversight* means supervision by someone responsible (*congressional oversight*, *a lack of oversight*). It also means a mistake made by not noticing something (*It was an oversight*).
entries.usage: Grammar usually separates the senses: supervision is uncountable (*oversight of the banks*), while the mistake is countable (*an oversight*, *a simple oversight*). *It was an oversight* is a polite, standard way to admit a small error. Related verbs: *oversee* (supervise) and *overlook* (fail to notice).
examples: A new independent board will provide **oversight** of the city's spending.
Sorry I left you off the invitation list; it was a complete **oversight**.
Without proper **oversight**, the construction company cut corners on safety.

drill.sentence: Forgetting to renew my passport before the trip was a silly {{oversight}} that almost cost me the vacation.
drill.hint: the word that also means supervision; here, a slip caused by not noticing

mistake.wrong: Sorry for my oversight of your email.
mistake.right: Sorry, I overlooked your email.
mistake.why: *Oversight of* something means supervising it; to say you missed it, use *overlook* or *It was an oversight*.

entries.label: usage trap
entries.meaning: *Invaluable* means extremely valuable, so useful that its value can't be measured. *Valueless* (or *worthless*) means having no value; the *in-* in *invaluable* does not mean *not*.
entries.usage: *Invaluable* is common praise for help, advice and experience (*Your feedback was invaluable*), close to *priceless*. The trap is like *flammable* and *inflammable*, which mean the same thing. For *of no value*, say *worthless* (common) or *valueless* (formal and rare).
examples: Her advice on negotiating my salary was **invaluable**.
After the company went bankrupt, its shares were essentially **valueless**.
A paper map is **invaluable** when you're hiking somewhere without cell service.

drill.sentence: Thanks for watching the kids last weekend; your help was {{invaluable}}.
drill.hint: invaluable or valueless? (extremely useful)

mistake.wrong: The painting turned out to be a fake, so it's invaluable.
mistake.right: The painting turned out to be a fake, so it's worthless.
mistake.why: *Invaluable* means extremely valuable; for something with no value, say *worthless* or *valueless*.

entries.label: US vs. UK
entries.meaning: In American English, to *table* a motion or proposal means postpone it or stop discussing it. In British English, it means the opposite: put it forward for discussion.
entries.usage: This difference causes real confusion in international meetings. In the US, *table* often means shelving an idea, sometimes for good, and it is common in everyday office talk (*Let's table that for now*). In British and Commonwealth usage, *table a proposal* means formally present it; with mixed audiences, say *postpone* or *put forward*.
examples: Let's **table** the budget discussion until next week's meeting.
The school board voted to **table** the proposal for a four-day week.
We **tabled** the idea of a family trip to Europe until the kids are older.

drill.sentence: We're out of time, so let's {{table}} this question and come back to it on Monday.
drill.hint: the meeting verb with opposite meanings in the US and the UK

mistake.wrong: I'd like to table my proposal today so we can vote on it.
mistake.right: I'd like to present my proposal today so we can vote on it.
mistake.why: In American meetings, *table* means postpone, so this sentence would say the opposite of what you mean.
